title: The Participation Paradox: Individual Agency and Rational Optimism in an Uncertain Society
content:
Socioeconomic Progress, Individual Agency, and the Value of Autonomy

INTRODUCTION

When a society becomes wealthier, does the individual necessarily become freer? Consider an employee who earns more after moving to a costly city, a government that spends billions on economic relief, and a consumer who gains access to technologies they played no part in developing. In each case, the apparent improvement can differ from the benefit an individual actually experiences. GDP, annual salary, program expenditure, and technological capability describe something important, but none alone determines the practical choices available to a person.

The distinction is visible in American fiscal history. The Economic Stimulus Act of 2008 issued direct payments to qualifying households; the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 distributed assistance through tax measures, safety-net programs, and public investment; and COVID-19 legislation combined household payments with support for employers and businesses. Each sought to stabilize economic activity, yet recipients encountered the programs in markedly different forms.[1][2][3]

These cases illustrate the broader participation paradox: individuals depend on collective systems for income, infrastructure, and technological opportunities, yet frequently use the resources they obtain to reduce the demands of continued participation. A higher salary may require longer hours and higher rent; a public investment may improve regional productivity while producing little directly observable benefit for a particular household. The gap between societal achievement and personal autonomy is not an accounting error. It is a central question about what progress is ultimately for.

Money is often treated as the objective of economic activity, but for many people it is primarily a means of purchasing security, leisure, mobility, or control over their future. Others genuinely value consumption, professional achievement, or visible wealth. The difference matters: if economic systems are evaluated only by what people earn, they overlook what people are trying to make possible with those earnings. The problem is not whether everyone shares one definition of success, but whether institutions leave room for individuals to pursue different definitions.

This essay argues that socioeconomic progress is not adequately assessed by the quantity of labor, money, or infrastructure generated alone. It must also be examined through its effect on individual capabilities: the realistic alternatives people possess, the obligations they must accept, and their ability to exercise discretion over time and resources. The essay develops this claim through technological diffusion, the economic cost of employment, historical fiscal interventions, and the individual response to structural constraints. Its interpretive framework, the Participation–Autonomy Paradox, is proposed as a synthesis, not as an empirically established law.

1. PROGRESS WITHOUT INDIVIDUAL PARTICIPATION

Can an individual advance without contributing proportionately to the advancement of society? In a literal sense, this happens routinely: scientific discoveries, manufacturing improvements, and infrastructure investments become available to people who neither invented nor financed them directly. But access is not automatic, and a newer technology is not necessarily a more useful one.

Over the past several decades, computers have become substantially more powerful, communication technologies more accessible, and numerous services considerably more efficient. An individual does not need to contribute directly to scientific research, engineering, or industrial production to benefit from these advances.

Kenneth Arrow's 1962 work on the economics of invention explored the economic characteristics of knowledge and technological innovation.[4] Subsequent research has examined how technological improvements spread beyond their original producers through competition, knowledge spillovers, and technological diffusion.

Consequently, the set of capabilities available to an individual can expand even when that individual contributes little to the underlying technological development. This is an improvement in opportunity, not necessarily in realized welfare. A person without the money, infrastructure, or skills needed to adopt the technology may capture little of the benefit.

However, technological development does not guarantee improved welfare. New products may be expensive, unreliable, poorly implemented, or difficult to access. Individuals must also maintain sufficient resources and adaptability to benefit from emerging technologies.

The significance for individual agency is that civilization can sometimes expand a person’s future options without requiring a comparable increase in that person’s own labor. Yet technological progress creates another dependency: taking advantage of new systems may require continuous learning, purchasing power, and institutional access. The paradox begins not with a prediction that the future will always improve, but with the difference between what society makes possible and what any individual can actually use.

2. THE ECONOMIC COST OF PARTICIPATION

Does moving for a higher salary make you better off, or merely more expensive to maintain? The question is partly economic and partly philosophical. Nominal income is observable, but the amount of life committed to earning it—and the costs necessary to remain in the relevant labor market—is harder to summarize.

Consider an employee who relocates to a major metropolitan area for a higher-paying position. Although their nominal salary increases, additional expenditures on housing, transportation, and necessities may absorb much of that advantage.

The relevant improvement is not simply a salary differential. It is the change in disposable resources, housing quality, commute, financial security, available time, and access to future opportunities after paying the costs required to earn that salary. Higher wages can be worthwhile, sometimes decisively so, but cannot be evaluated in isolation from those costs.

Economists Edward Glaeser and Joshua Gottlieb examined the relationships among productivity, wages, population, and housing prices in their 2009 research on agglomeration economies and spatial equilibrium.[5]

These relationships help explain why densely populated cities can provide substantially different economic opportunities and living standards despite sharing similar levels of population concentration.

Geographic mobility can become a form of adaptation to these constraints. Someone might seek employment in a high-wage economy, then retire or relocate to a region in which accumulated savings provide greater purchasing power. This separates, at least partly, the geographic location of wealth accumulation from the location of consumption. The benefit depends on migration costs, healthcare access, family ties, legal status, and the portability of income; it should not be assumed available to everyone.

The example connects individual choice to a larger institutional structure. A worker ordinarily cannot determine local wage levels or housing supply. They can sometimes choose among labor markets, renegotiate how they work, or reduce their expenses. The operative form of agency is often not redesigning the system but changing one’s position within it. That same logic will reappear when we examine employment, public assistance, and self-sufficiency.

3. THE PARTICIPATION-AUTONOMY PARADOX

What if someone doubles their income by doubling the time they spend working? A person earning $100,000 while working 80 hours a week has the same average gross hourly pay as someone earning $50,000 for 40 hours a week, assuming an equal number of working weeks. The higher earner still receives more money and may accumulate savings sooner. Yet the extra compensation is purchased with twice as many hours of labor. Annual income can conceal the time cost of obtaining it.

There are also nonmonetary limits. WHO and ILO analyses have associated working at least 55 hours per week with elevated risks of stroke and ischemic heart disease compared with 35–40 hours.[6] A series of studies by Tim Kasser and Kennon Sheldon found that perceived time affluence was positively associated with subjective well-being even when material affluence was taken into account.[7] Neither finding supplies a universal optimal workweek, but together they show why income alone cannot serve as a complete measure of the benefits of employment.

This distinction should not be confused with a claim that long hours always produce poor outcomes. A physician, entrepreneur, or worker temporarily taking a second job may rationally accept demanding hours for career development, debt reduction, or future independence. The question is whether the marginal benefit of that additional income justifies the accompanying loss of discretionary time, recovery, and flexibility.

The popular advice to enjoy one's twenties rather than spend them working illustrates the same conflict at a different scale. Leisure postponed cannot always be recovered in precisely the same form, yet a person struggling to meet rent or establish an emergency fund cannot simply choose unrestricted leisure. Saving aggressively may improve future options, but exhausting the present in pursuit of distant independence has its own cost. A defensible comparison must therefore include both the security created by earnings and the opportunity cost of years spent earning them, not merely the eventual age at which someone can afford to stop.

Work can also become an end rather than a means. Someone may pursue financial independence through employment so demanding that the present freedom they hoped eventually to secure is substantially reduced. Another person may prefer a predictable, moderately engaging job that leaves energy for interests and relationships outside work. Still another may find genuine meaning and autonomy in a demanding career. These are different preference structures, not evidence that one occupational identity is universally correct.

The distinction is between wealth accumulation and the exercise of freedom. Wealth can expand future choices; the pursuit of wealth can also consume present choices. Whether that exchange is worthwhile depends on compensation, health, time horizon, obligations, and what the individual values beyond work.

What does an additional dollar buy if the work required to earn it leaves no time to use it? The answer differs between a worker struggling to cover essentials and an individual who already has ample savings. In the first case, additional income may provide crucial security; in the second, the value of free time or reduced exposure to an exhausting job may be greater. Money can therefore be an instrument of autonomy without autonomy being reducible to money. It is precisely this distinction that makes the quantity of hours worked an incomplete measure of economic success.

Credit introduces a second version of this temporal trade-off. A credit card or a buy-now-pay-later plan can permit consumption before the next paycheck arrives, which may help households manage mismatched income and expenses. But borrowing is a claim on future resources, not an increase in net worth. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau found that multiple simultaneous buy-now-pay-later loans were common among users in its 2022 dataset, highlighting why payment flexibility and long-term affordability should not be conflated.[8] Such products can increase immediate discretion while reducing future discretion through repayment obligations.

At the more extreme end, social-media jokes about spending to the limit of one's credit and treating bankruptcy—or even relocation—as an effortless escape reveal the appeal of independence from financial obligation. The premise is misleading. U.S. bankruptcy is a legal process that can discharge certain debts but not all of them; discharge can be contested, including in cases involving fraud, and leaving a location is not itself a bankruptcy discharge.[9] Freedom financed entirely through new liabilities may amount to a transfer of constraint from the present to the future.

Albert O. Hirschman's 1970 book, Exit, Voice, and Loyalty, provides a relevant theoretical framework. Hirschman distinguished between attempting to improve an unsatisfactory institution and withdrawing from it.[10]

This distinction applies to workers who change occupations, individuals who relocate, and people who pursue financial independence rather than attempting to modify the larger institutions governing their circumstances.

Psychologists Richard Ryan and Edward Deci have likewise emphasized autonomy as a fundamental component of human motivation and well-being through Self-Determination Theory.[11]

The Participation–Autonomy Paradox describes this double role of economic participation: labor and institutional membership create the resources needed for independence, but can impose the very demands from which independence is sought. The paradox is not that work is irrational. It is that the resources gained and freedom surrendered must be evaluated together, rather than treating greater income as synonymous with greater welfare.

A useful alternative to the imperative to maximize earnings is the idea of economic sufficiency: obtaining enough security and opportunity that additional work becomes a choice rather than an immediate necessity. The threshold will differ among individuals and can change as family, health, or financial obligations change. That variability is part of the argument, not an exception to it.

4. COLLECTIVE PROGRESS AND UNINTENDED CONSEQUENCES

When government announces billions of dollars in spending, what exactly has improved for the ordinary person? National output, employment, and infrastructure can change without each household experiencing the same improvement. The distinction becomes concrete when comparing roads and public facilities with payments or credit that eligible recipients can use directly. Historical U.S. fiscal policy provides a useful test of this difference.

4.1 PUBLIC INVESTMENT: HIGHWAYS, INFRASTRUCTURE, AND COLLECTIVE BENEFITS

Few frustrations make the costs of metropolitan life as visible as sitting in traffic. The intuitive solution sounds simple: if the highway is crowded, why not add another lane? More road capacity should give drivers more room and shorten their commutes. But what happens when easier driving attracts additional trips? Commuters can switch routes or travel times, and over longer periods some households and businesses may change where they locate. The proposed solution changes the incentives that created the original problem.

In 1956, President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act, accelerating the construction of the United States Interstate Highway System. The legislation authorized $25 billion for Interstate construction over fiscal years 1957 through 1969, with the federal government covering 90 percent of eligible construction costs.[12] The resulting network expanded intercity mobility and commercial connections, but its effects were not universally beneficial: urban expressway construction also displaced neighborhoods, redirected commerce, and helped reshape residential development around automobile travel.[13]

A more recent example is the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, signed by President Joe Biden in November 2021. Commonly called the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, it authorized approximately $1.2 trillion in transportation and infrastructure spending, including roughly $550 billion in new investments. Its provisions cover more than highways, extending to areas such as bridges, water systems, energy, and broadband infrastructure.[14]

Economists Gilles Duranton and Matthew Turner investigated this feedback effect in their 2011 study of American cities. They found that increases in Interstate highway capacity were associated with roughly proportional increases in vehicle travel, a result consistent with induced demand.[15] This does not mean that every additional lane is useless: added capacity can accommodate valuable travel, connect communities, and support commerce. But it means that new asphalt cannot, by itself, guarantee permanently shorter commutes. The aggregate achievement of moving more vehicles is not identical to the individual experience of spending less time in traffic.

The broader socioeconomic question is therefore not simply how much infrastructure a government builds, but which benefits remain available to particular individuals after people respond to it. A new bridge or highway is physically tangible, yet its value is distributed across users, locations, and years. Someone who never uses the bridge may still receive indirect benefits through commerce or services, while an everyday commuter may experience benefits different from those suggested by the amount spent. This distinction is not an argument against public investment. It is an argument for separating measurable collective output from realized individual welfare—the same distinction that matters when assessing income, employment, or government assistance.

4.2 DIRECT RELIEF: THE STIMULUS PAYMENTS OF 2008, 2009, AND 2020-2021

Direct fiscal assistance provides a contrasting example because the individual can often identify its immediate monetary value. Under the Economic Stimulus Act of 2008, signed by President George W. Bush, eligible taxpayers received payments of up to $600 individually or $1,200 for married couples filing jointly, with an additional amount for qualifying children. The payments were distinct from ordinary tax refunds and were subject to eligibility rules and income phaseouts.[1]

The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 (ARRA), signed by President Barack Obama, used a broader combination of fiscal mechanisms in response to the Great Recession. The Congressional Budget Office initially estimated its deficit impact at $787 billion over fiscal years 2009 through 2019, later revising the estimate to nearly $840 billion. Rather than consisting exclusively of stimulus checks, it combined household tax relief, extended unemployment assistance, increased federal support for Medicaid and education, and spending on transportation and other investments.[2]

One of its more familiar provisions was the Making Work Pay tax credit: up to $400 per eligible worker or $800 for married joint filers in each of 2009 and 2010. For many employed recipients, the benefit appeared through lower federal income tax withholding rather than a separate lump-sum check. The Act also provided one-time $250 payments to certain Social Security, Supplemental Security Income, veterans, and other benefit recipients.[16]

More than a decade later, the COVID-19 emergency produced three widely recognized rounds of Economic Impact Payments: up to $1,200 per eligible adult under the March 2020 CARES Act, up to $600 under legislation enacted in December 2020, and up to $1,400 under the March 2021 American Rescue Plan Act. The treatment of qualifying children and other dependents differed by round, and eligibility was subject to income and other conditions.[3]

A qualifying recipient could choose to apply a $1,400 payment toward groceries, rent, debt, or savings. The monetary assistance is visible, and the discretion over its use can be valuable. An equal amount of spending on public infrastructure or specialized services may be more difficult for the same individual to identify as a personal benefit, even when the social benefit is substantial. This distinction between personal discretion, benefit incidence, and aggregate impact is central to the essay.

4.3 SMALL-BUSINESS RELIEF: PPP, EIDL, AND THE PRICE OF SPEED

The COVID-19 response also provided a less straightforward example of direct assistance. The CARES Act established the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), which offered loans intended to help eligible employers retain workers and cover specified expenses; qualifying loans could be forgiven when program requirements were satisfied.[17] The COVID-19 Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) program provided loans that generally had to be repaid, while certain EIDL advances did not require repayment.[18] These are different arrangements: a forgivable loan, a repayable loan, and a grant-like advance should not all be described simply as free government money.

The objective was to preserve employment and business continuity amid an emergency. But speed and ease of access introduced oversight risks. In a March 2025 review, the Government Accountability Office reported that SBA had made or guaranteed more than $1 trillion in pandemic loans and grants to over ten million businesses and found that core antifraud procedures were implemented only after a large share of funding had already been approved or disbursed. GAO also reported that nearly two million of roughly three million potential COVID-EIDL fraud referrals could not be fully investigated because of missing, inaccurate, or duplicative information.[19] Referral counts and fraud indicators, however, must not be mistaken for proven fraudulent transactions.

The risk was not merely theoretical. In a December 2025 federal case, prosecutors reported that a defendant had used fictitious business entities and stolen identifying information in a scheme involving fraudulent PPP and EIDL applications; the defendant was sentenced to prison.[20] The point of including this example is not that business relief was generally fraudulent. It is that a program designed to deliver immediate, tangible benefits to legitimate businesses can also be exploited if accountability does not keep pace with distribution.

This creates a genuine policy trade-off. Extensive verification may delay assistance to employers and workers in urgent need, while permissive distribution can divert funds away from intended recipients and impose later investigation and recovery costs. The individual-benefit perspective is therefore insufficient on its own: public assistance must be evaluated by its accessibility, its effects on legitimate recipients, and the institutional capacity needed to maintain trust and prevent abuse.

4.4 DOES A MORE VISIBLE BENEFIT PRODUCE A BETTER ECONOMIC OUTCOME?

Economic research suggests that the method of delivery can affect consumer behavior. Claudia Sahm, Matthew Shapiro, and Joel Slemrod compared household responses to the one-time 2008 stimulus payments and the 2009 Making Work Pay tax credit. Their survey-based estimates indicated a higher short-run spending response to the lump-sum payments, approximately 25 percent, than to the tax relief delivered largely through reduced withholding, approximately 13 percent. The policies also operated under different circumstances, so this comparison should not be treated as proof that the delivery method alone caused the difference.[21]

Research on the 2020 Economic Impact Payments likewise found substantial variation across households. Jonathan Parker and coauthors reported that many households spent only a small fraction of the first payment shortly after receiving it, while households with fewer liquid financial resources or greater exposure to pandemic-related income disruptions tended to increase consumption more. A payment can therefore be highly visible and personally useful without generating the same immediate spending response for every recipient.[22]

These episodes should not be reduced to the question of whether a stimulus check feels better than a new bridge. They raise several analytically separate issues: who qualifies for assistance; who ultimately benefits; when those benefits occur; how recipients respond; and what institutional safeguards are needed to deliver the intended result. Direct payments can preserve individual discretion. Infrastructure may generate widespread benefits that no single recipient could purchase alone. Business relief can protect payroll while also exposing weaknesses in verification. The policy choice depends on objectives, opportunity costs, and evidence, not merely on whether its benefit is immediately tangible to a particular person.

5. BEYOND AGGREGATE ECONOMIC INDICATORS

Are we improving lives, or just improving the scoreboard? GDP, employment, national income, and infrastructure expenditures measure important aspects of an economy, but they do not fully determine whether individuals have more practical options, less financial insecurity, or greater control over their time. A country may report stronger growth while some households experience rising housing costs or deteriorating access to essential services.

Amartya Sen's capability approach, developed extensively in Development as Freedom, argues that economic development should be evaluated partly through the substantive freedoms and opportunities available to individuals.[23]

Similarly, economist Marc Fleurbaey examined alternatives to conventional economic measures in his 2009 paper, Beyond GDP: The Quest for a Measure of Social Welfare.[24]

Even the evaluation of an emergency policy can require separating national results from the experiences of particular households. In its retrospective analysis of the 2009 Recovery Act, the Congressional Budget Office evaluated estimated changes in GDP and employment relative to a hypothetical economy without the legislation. Such aggregate estimates are not interchangeable with the benefit received by any one worker, taxpayer, or consumer.[2]

These perspectives raise a more precise question than whether growth is good or bad: under what conditions does an increase in aggregate productive capacity become an expansion of individual freedom? A society can generate more economic output without distributing its benefits equally, while an individual can improve personal welfare through lower expenses, mobility, or greater discretionary time without producing more output.

Someone earning less money may enjoy lower expenses, fewer obligations, greater geographic flexibility, and more control over personal time than someone receiving substantially higher compensation.

Neither arrangement is universally preferable. Higher income can provide important forms of security and freedom, while reduced participation can introduce financial vulnerability.

The practical implication is not to abandon aggregate measures but to supplement them with measures of financial security, health, discretionary time, access, and choice. The criterion of success changes from an unquestioned imperative to produce more toward an inquiry into what additional production actually enables people to do.

What individuals call financial independence also varies. For one person, it means sufficient savings to reject unfavorable employment; for another, the ability to travel, raise a family, start a venture, or enjoy ordinary leisure without constant financial pressure. Visible status consumption is another preference, but not the necessary endpoint of earning more. The economic question is not whether one lifestyle is morally superior, but whether income, institutions, and personal resources create workable choices among these different ends.

6. INDIVIDUAL AGENCY WITHIN LARGER SYSTEMS

What should an individual do when the conditions shaping their life are largely beyond their control? This is the philosophical problem beneath the economic examples. No single person can set global energy prices, eliminate a geopolitical conflict, direct national productivity, or determine when the next transformative technology will become available.

Yet the absence of control over an outcome does not eliminate agency within the circumstances. Individuals can modify expenses, develop skills, select occupations, relocate where feasible, retain savings, or prepare for service disruptions. These actions may not change the larger system, but can change a person’s exposure to its risks and their ability to benefit from its opportunities.

Hirschman’s distinction between voice and exit helps clarify the alternatives. A person can try to alter an institution, withdraw from it, or remain while negotiating its constraints. None is universally rational: changing a rule can improve conditions for many people, while leaving a harmful arrangement can be the more feasible choice for one person. Structural constraints also mean that not everyone has equal access to relocation, savings, or occupational mobility.

The relationship between individuals and institutions is therefore neither simple dependence nor simple antagonism. Governments establish and enforce rules for markets and workplaces, while citizens, workers, and firms respond to those rules in different ways. Complaints, voting, litigation, organizing, and protest are forms of attempted institutional change, but none guarantees a particular result; leaving a job or moving away may offer more immediate relief to one person while doing little to resolve the underlying problem for others. Hirschman’s framework is useful precisely because it distinguishes the costs and possibilities of voice from those of exit, without assuming either will always succeed.

Nor is prioritizing personal autonomy automatically equivalent to ethical egoism or indifference toward other people. The desire to leave a hostile workplace, preserve health, or obtain more discretionary time is compatible with concern for coworkers, family, and public welfare. A person may decide that organizing for reform is worth the effort; another may conclude that changing employers is a more feasible response. The broader social value of collective action and the privately feasible choice for a constrained individual are different questions. Treating them as identical obscures both.

What does freedom of employment choice mean when some advertised opportunities may not actually be available? The Congressional Research Service addressed “ghost” job postings in a 2025 report, defining them as listings for jobs that do not exist or that an employer does not plan to fill immediately. The report identified several possible causes: collecting applications for future use, signaling growth, advertising a role while anticipating an internal hire, and postings that remain online after circumstances change. It also noted that there is no official estimate of how widespread the practice is.[25] A job seeker can spend hours evaluating and applying for a position, yet have limited information about whether an actual vacancy exists. This is an institutional information asymmetry with a real personal opportunity cost—not evidence that every unfilled listing is intentionally deceptive.

This example returns the argument to its starting point. Economic freedom depends not only on an individual’s willingness to improve their circumstances, but also on the reliability of the opportunities that institutions present. Financial savings, skills, and mobility increase a person’s available options, while transparency and credible rules affect how usable those options actually are. Neither self-improvement nor institutional reform is a complete substitute for the other.

A philosophical parallel appears in Stoicism. Epictetus distinguished judgments and choices from external circumstances that do not rest within the individual’s power.[26] Applied cautiously to modern life, that distinction encourages attention to decisions one can make without pretending that geopolitical events, inflation, or institutional failures are imaginary. Stoic discipline is not a substitute for public policy or collective action. It is one possible response to the gap between personal control and external uncertainty.

Another response is to reduce dependence on vulnerable infrastructure. Individuals may try to retain backup electricity, water supplies, food reserves, or more independent housing. Underground shelter designs are a particularly striking—if costly—architectural illustration of this impulse: a private attempt to preserve usable space and essential services when external systems fail.


Figure 1. Underground survival bunker illustrating residential self-sufficiency and technological dependence. Design reference: DEFCON Underground Mfg.

The shelter also reveals a deeper dependence. Its air filtration, electronics, construction materials, and engineering principles come from the accumulated work of the larger society it is designed to withstand disruptions from. Finite supplies, equipment maintenance, healthcare, and replacement parts limit how autonomous such a space can be. The objective is therefore more realistically understood as resilience or selective dependence, not guaranteed indefinite survival.

This is the participation paradox in another form. Collective technological development can make private self-sufficiency more feasible, but self-sufficiency itself rests on collective achievements. The individual does not escape the social system completely; they use its products to create some distance from its immediate vulnerabilities.

An emphasis on agency need not entail blaming individuals for every hardship, just as recognizing structural problems need not imply that an individual can solve them. The useful distinction is between what collective institutions ought to address and what a particular person can realistically change. Autonomy is meaningful precisely because available choices are constrained, unevenly distributed, and sometimes costly to exercise.

7. CONCLUSION: A RATIONAL BASIS FOR OPTIMISM

If the future is uncertain and individuals control so little of it, is pessimism the more rational position? Not necessarily. The historical cases in this essay demonstrate both the vulnerability and the adaptability of socioeconomic systems: relief programs can stabilize households yet invite abuse; highways can create opportunities yet alter travel behavior; technology can broaden possibilities without ensuring equal access. Uncertainty is not evidence that favorable outcomes are impossible, nor is past progress proof that they are guaranteed.

The relevant form of optimism is neither blind faith in growth nor a prediction that technology will solve every social problem. It is a conditional judgment: an individual may benefit from future advances they did not cause and may preserve meaningful agency by keeping options open. That judgment becomes more defensible when paired with savings, flexibility, health, institutional accountability, and realistic attention to risks.

It is tempting to regard wealth as proof of success and political or institutional frustration as proof of powerlessness. Both conclusions move too quickly. Personal prosperity can consist partly in freedom from unwanted obligations, while effective agency can consist of selective adaptation as well as attempts at collective change. A defensible optimism does not promise justice or security merely because time passes; it recognizes that preserving options and improving institutions can make favorable outcomes more attainable.

Technological developments can expand human capabilities independently of individual contributions. Geographic mobility can improve purchasing power without requiring institutional reform. Financial independence, reduced consumption, and technological adoption may provide greater autonomy without corresponding increases in labor or productivity.

This does not erase the force of inequality, economic disruption, illness, or involuntary obligations. Nor does it mean that reducing work or moving away is possible for everyone. The freedom to adapt is itself a resource distributed unevenly across society, which is why public institutions and collective action remain relevant alongside personal strategies.

Nevertheless, uncertainty contains the possibility of favorable developments as well as unfavorable ones.

A rationally optimistic individual need not assume civilization will advance without interruption. They can instead distinguish trends that are outside their control from choices still available within those trends, while avoiding the mistake of treating nominal wealth, aggregate output, or sheer hours worked as sufficient measures of a life going well.

The Participation Paradox ultimately concerns the relationship between the individual's contribution to society and the benefits, obligations, and opportunities produced by society.

Its central proposition is that socioeconomic progress should not be evaluated solely by how much individuals produce or consume, but also by how much freedom they possess to determine the conditions of their participation.

Socioeconomic progress acquires personal significance when it increases an individual’s feasible choices—not merely when it increases the amount produced, spent, or earned. The ability to benefit from collective progress without being compelled to maximize one’s contribution to it may itself be an important dimension of individual welfare.

Under this interpretation, optimism does not mean assuming the future must improve. It means recognizing that limited control over the future does not exhaust the possibilities for improving one’s position within it. The paradox is that modern systems can simultaneously demand participation and produce the tools with which individuals gain greater freedom from that demand.

AUTHOR'S NOTE

This essay is an interpretive synthesis of established research in economics, psychology, public policy, and philosophy. The Participation–Autonomy Paradox is a proposed conceptual framework, not an empirically validated law. Historical cases are illustrations of mechanisms and trade-offs, not proof that one level of employment or one form of public expenditure is optimal for everyone.

title: The Wiggle That Killed Tarkov
content:
Credit: g0at

Tarkov player goes undercover with ESP (extra sensory perception; wallhacks) and wiggles to find other wallhackers. g0at, the creator of this YouTube video, goes on the first person shooter survival game, Escape from Tarkov, and pretends to be a cheater in order to find cheaters. Even though he is using a wallhack cheat, he is not using other hacks like aimbot or flying around. Furthermore, g0at does not shoot other players nor does he loot other players. In game, when he is near enough another player, he tests them for cheating. He leans left and right, which is a movement mechanic normally used to peek around corners, or to indicate friendliness. He 'wiggles', facing walls, even though a legitimate player would not be able to see the movement. On the other end, cheaters who use wallhacks will see him peek, although they have to decide whether or not to 'reveal' themselves as seeing g0at through the wall that is blocking both players' views. g0at pretends to be friendly, continues following suspicious players, and even gets a few cheaters to admit to hacking. However not all of the cheating players wave back, and instantly take a shot at g0at when he is in clear view. This video shows how playing competitive games is not really fun, as cheaters will always exist, and there is nothing non-cheaters can do about it.

title: The Online Chess Cheating Problem
content:
If you don't have the time to read this, here is a picture: Reddit
What it says is that 15.7% of online chess players are cheaters, and over 20% have admitted to cheating in the past. Does this mean everyone online is a cheater? No, especially not at the lower levels, below 1600 elo. Losing points, not improving, and wasting time is not worth the effort.

Chess is one of the oldest board games that had recorded games as early as the 16th century, coinciding with the birth of Ruy López de Segura, of Spain, who was known as the best player of early chess. Ruy López popularized the most famous Chess opening known as the Ruy Lopez, or Spanish game, that starts with:

1. e4 e5, 2. nf3 nc6, 3. bb5 ... , undermining Black's knight or defense of the center e pawn, and giving white a slight initiative. Even today, Chess is still played throughout the world, and is even mandatory in Armenia for school children. Chess is also played online on sites like Chess.com and Lichess.org, which can have over 50,000 games being played at the same time, per platform. Chess is also popularized in the modern age by the Queen's Gambit movie, which was a 2020 fiction drama movie starring Anya Taylor-Joy who played Beth Harmon, a top fenmale chess player.

So then, where does Chess fall off? To a newer player of the game, who might have played a couple of games with their friends in the past, or someone who has watched the Queen's Gambit movie, it is very difficult to tell that up to 20% of their online opponents are actual cheaters. First of all, online chess is completely free to play. Players can make as many accounts as they would like. However, players can not cheat as they like, since cheating is a bannable offense. Therefore, all a cheater needs to do is load up a chess engine as a browser extension or on their phone, not blatantly look up and play the best move for every match they play, and they will have an unfair advantage after the first couple of opening moves for the rest of the game.

For example, 'Chessvision.ai' is a Chrome extension that has over 100,000 users. The description says:'Analyze chess positions from any website, book, and video in Chrome | Automatically analyze chess positions on any website and video you want.' This extension automatically scans for any chess board, detects the current position on the board, and opens up a mini-window that shows an engine evaluation of the current position. Keep in mind the 100,000 users number, this is only a single example tool that anyone can use for free online. There are dozens of alternative extension or software cheating tools to choose from.

title: Starcraft 2: A Deteriorating Mess
content:
Starcraft 2, or sc2, has been known as one of the most popular RTS (real time strategy) games, the newer rendition of the original Starcraft series, which was released in 2010 and saw popularity from 2012-2016 until losing popularity to newer games like Counter Strike, League of Legends, and Fortnite. However, the days of Sc2 are long over, and Sc2's developer, Blizzard Entertainment, has never looked back. Moreover, once Sc2's multiplayer 1v1 mode was made free to play on November 2017, this was the start of Sc2's downfall. For veteran players, the multiplayer player pool, or ladder, was swarmed with mostly new players who had no other sense of the game other than watching pro players play or their friends. Starcraft 2 is not an easy game to play, it is certainly not beginner friendly. No matter how many hours a new player has watched the game, new players need a minimum of 100 hours in the game to learn the controls and how to not lose instantly when being matched against a real opponent. To win consistently against real opponents in the middle 50th percentile? Well atleast 500 hours watched and played in game.

I myself have put in atleast 500 hours in the game played, and maybe 500 hours watching YouTube videos and Twitch streams. In 2018 I reached Diamond 3, or the top 25% of players on the NA ladder. However, I stopped playing and returned to the game in 2021 and 2025. What do you think happened once Blizzard made the game free to play? Well, the short answer is that the current 1v1 ladder in 2025 is flooded with veterans, sandbaggers, and smurfs, which makes the game extremely difficult to play for new players but even experienced players that aren't sandbagging their actual rating.

What is Sandbagging? Sandbagging is a term used in gaming where a player deliberately lowers their rating by leaving matches or losing games on purpose in order to get matched against lower rated opponents. The result of sandbagging is that if you are currently rated 3000 rating points on the ladder, if you get matched against a sandbagger (or smurf), you will be at an unfair disadvantage. First of all, you do not know your opponent's actual rating, and you also do not know that they are playing below their actual rating, atleast until you end up losing the game, when it's already too late.

For clarification, the difference between smurfs and sandbaggers is that smurfs deliberately make multiple accounts that aren't their main account in order to conceal or freeze their main account's top rating. So although smurfing is not technically cheating or hacking, it gives smurfs an unfair advantage, equivalent to match fixing in professional sports, or rating manipulation, which are bannable offenses. Since Blizzard has not addressed the issues of smurfing and sandbagging, there has been no improvement since 2017. I would estimate the current percentage of smurfs/sandbaggers to be at least 20% of the players in the range of 2700-4000 MMR (Match making rating) rating points, peaking at 33% during certain times of the day, such as late at night or during weekdays.

So what is actually going on, then? Well, since I am currently at 2900 MMR, or Platinum 2, up to 33% of my games are playing against smurfs and sandbaggers who are actually 3300-3600 MMR points, which nearly guarantees that the game will end in an unfair loss. What sandbaggers/smurfs do is that they leave 4-7 games in a row, or atleast one game for every game they won, when their account is currently under 500 MMR their main account or actual rating. As a result, they will always be getting matched against players who are weaker than them, and win, depending on how many games they decide to leave. Since the other 70% of players are not smurfs or sandbaggers, the only way they can lose is if they get matched against another smurf/sandbagger, which might occur in less than 5-10% of total games, and isn't a problem for the smurf/sandbagger. Keep in mind that the match making system does not address smurfs and sandbaggers, so it doesn't mean that a player going on a win streak is going to get matched against another player going on a win streak. In fact, the only reason I was able to get promoted from Gold 2 to Platinum 3 was having to both play better than my actual rating, and not get matched against smurfs and sandbaggers. If Blizzard did actually address the sandbagger smurf problem with Sc2, I would actually be in Diamond 2 at this point, and not have to be stuck in Platinum 2.

title: Chess, What I Learned
content:
My Lichess Rating
Even though online Chess is not guaranteed to be clean, I have probably played some brilliant moves on Chess.com and not regretted it. The picture shows that I indeed have a rating over 2000, but I haven't played for a couple of months as of this date. This post will serve as general advice towards new players who are interested in playing Chess, specifically online chess in the rapid time category. Chess is a game of memorization, pattern recognition, and positional initiative. Each player starts out with their pieces on their starting squares. Original chess theory before the modern age of chess hypothesized that moving your center pawns forward towards the center of the board was a way to claim positional space on the board, which increases the moveability of your own pieces while at the same time cramping your opponent's pieces. Since your pawns can only forward, they are the weakest piece in the opening. Moving your center pawn forward gives each of your other pieces more space to develop and move out of their opening positions. This e4 or d4 move in the opning is considered good for challenging your opponent's center, which gives your pieces better attacking chances and more initiative. This is a vast generalization of the idea behind e4/d4, but it might make sense if you are starting to learn the game. Later on, chess theory turned more towards g6 or nf6 as black if your white opponent goes e4 or d4, respectively. The idea behind this is that there is no longer the 1. e4-e5 tension in the center, which allows a slightly more diverse set of opening choices for black that isn't fighting for the center. Instead of e5, black goes g6 and then bg7, which fianchettos the black dark squared bishop and prepares for king side castling. In addition, the bishop on g7 is eying the center d4 square, which white would like to place their pawn after e4 for more center space. This opening is called the modern opening, where white goes e4, then d4 or nf3, and black responds with g6 and bg7. While white is claiming space in the center, black is responding with a quick king side castle defense and attacking the center indirectly with its dark square bishop on g7. For beginners, keep in mind that pushing e4 e5 d4 d5 might undermine your center defense in the middlegame, as center pawns are also the easiest to target. Black's idea in the opening is to quickly develop its pieces to allow it to castle king side or queenside. White's idea is to gain space in the center, to later potentially give it better attacking chances towards Black's king.

to an intermediate player, this advice sounds too basic, so let me turn to more advanced topics around my rating range. Disregard if your rating is much higher than mines as this should already be familiar territory. In the middlegame, many players lack a plan to either go after your opponent's king or try to further undermine/cramp your opponent's pieces/position. Some players might miss an important tactical shot in the middlegame, which could be potentially game changing. For example, as white if black pins your c3 knight or f3 knight with their corresponding bishops on b4/g4, white can always reply with a3,b4 or h3, g4 to kick the bishop and take more space on the sides of the board. Even though h3/g4 weakens the kingside castling position, it allows for more attacking chances. Similarly, if you are playing black and white pins your f6 knight with bg5, h6 and g5 can be a good attacking response in certain lines. If both sides have castled kingside, black can usually play h6/g5 to play a kingside pawn storm attack towards white's king.

As White, I have a preference for 1.d4 openings, specifically the Catalan opening, or the Jobava-London. If black doesn't respond properly and immediately try to play e5 nc6, white will have a comfortable opening and easy to play middlegame. If you don't know what these openings are, it's basically a Queen's Gambit Declined (QGD) with white's light squared bishop fianchettoed on g3 in addition. This opening gives white center pawn control, center pawn reinforcement from the fianchettoed bishop, and a sound kingside castle. The Catalan has been played at the highest levels of chess recently, and thats why I also like it.

As black, I usually play g6, the Modern, in response to 1. e4. If white brazingly tries to attack and center pawn storm without developing enough their other pieces, they sometimes fumble defense of a pawn and their stack of card pawn structure usually collapses. However, be wary of later h4 moves, as a good attacking player will be able to attack and take initiative before their center position starts to weaken. 1.d4 nf6! is another common idea for black, as its the most popular opening response to d4 for black. D6 is also another transposing opening choice against d4, but I feel like it is too passive and gives white a more comfortable opening position. The way to win games above the beginner level is to restrict your opponent's moves, pressure the weaknesses in their position (pawn breaks), and seize the initiative in the position when given the chance. However, as I mentioned before, you need to understands and 'see' the middlegame patterns for when there's a tactic or when there's a certain weakness in your opponents position that can be exploited.

if you manage to make it to the endgame versus an equally rated opponent, it's even more necessary to overdefend your minor pieces or center pawns as rooks can quickly target weak pawns and scoop them up from the side files or even behind your overpushed/weak exposed pawns. I would say I have lost many games in an equal position due to overlooking a two-move combo from my opponents rook that would quickly slide from the back towards the sides of the board and attack my pawns aligned horziontally past the middle ranks. Theres a common technique to cutoff the king where you slide your rooks to the seventh rank, preventing your opponent's king from marching towards the center and being able to escort their passed pawns. Stockfish sometimes gives +-5 just from a cutoff king, as there is both the threat of being checkmated on the last rank as well as not being able to promote or defend their passed pawns.

Knights are the most dangerous in short time controls or time pressure, as it's easy to fork a rook and king at the same time when there aren't many pieces on the board.

for lower rated players or beginners, I would also recommend th Pirc Defense, as it gives an alternative center counter towards e4-e5 that isn't as passive as e6 or g6. The Scandinavian Defense is also an annoying center-counter response to your opponent if they were just planning on going e4, d4, e5. It's a more advanced variation that is more dangerous for beginners, as center queens can quickly be activated, so I wouldn't recommend it completely. Knight outposts in the middlegame are also very annoying to deal with. If they can't be kicked with a pawn, or the pawns forming the knight outpost, then knights on outposts are worth atleast a rook, especially if they are towards the center or your opponent's king. If you want to play it safe, develop your pieces enough so that center knights can be traded off by bishops or atleast kicked away by h6 or h3.

title: Starcraft 2 Gold/Platinum Terran Guide
content:
My Sc2 Rating
I am now Diamond 3 on the NA ladder, or about 3140 MMR. This puts me at about top 25% of NA Starcraft 2 players, so I would say I have some experience playing the game as the Terran race.

To start, I will say that the NA ladder has the stereotype of being more cheesy than the other EU and KR servers, meaning you will face more early aggressive builds that are meant to quickly crush their opponent. However, don't worry if you are losing to cheese as a beginner, it's one way to learn how the mechanics of the game work and where your build order or strategy is weak. As a terran, it's not easy to play bio (marines, marauders, medivacs) near the midgame and lategame, as bio requires a very fast and micro-intensive playstyle. For example, if you open standard reaper fast expand against zerg, you will need to micro your reapar to both pressure the zergs natural as well as being able to build your factory at 100 gas. If you only do one or the other, chances are you will quickly fall behind of your opponent. So for beginners, playing marine first into reactor is less micro intensive and much easier to play. However, your first reaper will importantly scout against early ling pressure, baneling bust, or two base roach all-ins. The main idea for terran bio against zerg is to send out 1/2 marine medivac drops to clear creep and deny new expansions. Terran, as bio, must be proactive enough to drop both sides of the map at once, and setup tank pushes at the same time. If not, zerg will be comfortable enough to go to brood lord/viper/infestor, which shuts down tank pushes immediately. If the zerg goes multiple spores in their main, or goes muta/ling/bane, then drop play should only be for clearing creep or denying expansions, dropping in the main or naturals is usually not worth it.

Against terran I would go reaper reaper hellion, but defensively until your hellion is finished. Try to take out your opponent's reaper or 2 scvs if possible. Next would be reactored marines, one or two cyclones, and tanks/raven afterward. An early cyclone helps shut down one base medivac drops and can kill reaper reaper hellion. If you're not comfortable playing ravens, then don't, play vikings instead. Vikings will beat poorly microed ravens, medivacs, liberators, and even battlecruisers, if given the chance. So marine tank viking as bio, just keep your macro and upgrades in check. Always have atleast 2 barracks for each expansion you have, to ensure you won't get completely wiped out if your marines accidentally walk into tank fire.

One important note to mention, in TvT, make sure you watch out for a two base battlecruiser build, one base tank drop build, or proxies. Since pro players play bio instead of mech in 75% of games, bio is what I play, but if you like mech, then go for it. Mech is good against zerg, but against a tactical bio player or protoss you can be easily outpositioned or outplayed. I actually think mech is the better build for players under diamond, as tank/viking doesn't require much micro and defense is easier.

If you play against protoss, go normal 1rax/reactor into delayed proxy double marauders, just make sure the protoss player doesn't see the two proxy scvs leaving your base - this is how I reached diamond with a 70% winrate vs protoss. Similarly, against zerg, you can go for the proxy 4 rax marines build. The proxy 4 rax is very strong against weaker opponents, and even if the zerg defends their main with spines, you will just bunker contain their natural and followup with a normal expansion into tank push. After the first rax is finished, that scv will immediately build the fourth rax. Rally each scv 12s in-between across the map to ensure efficient build timing and mineral expenditure/mining. If you're smart, you would rally your scvs around the shortest overlord scout path and slightly past your opponents fourth expansion. I would say that with proper execution, no zerg player under gold 1 should be able to fully defend or figure out the correct followup if they manage to defend their main. Just ensure the zerg doesn't sneak out zerglings across the map and make sure to build the 3 supply depots to blockade your main ramp. In standard reaper fast expand vs zerg, you can also choose to wall off your natural base instead of your main ramp if you want. Just keep in mind this is more risky against baneling busts and 2-base roach attacks before your tank is able to finish. However if you manage to keep your reaper alive, you will quickly understand the importance of the reaper in the build.

For scouting against terran and zerg, you can rally a scv from your main to your opponent's ramp when your rax is about 40% finished. You can also optionally scout your third expansion first for proxies (against terran) before rallying to your opponent's ramp. Against protoss, you don't really need to scout, the reason being you should always put a bunker at your natural to defend against early adept/stalker prsesure. Going 2/1/1 cyclone first helps deny proxy voids, and raven first helps deny DTs. Two-base marine/marauder tank medivac all-in with 5-10 scvs pulled or mine drop would be my build recommendations against protoss if you choose to play standard instead. Just make sure stim finishes and your scvs pad for your tank, you can set your scvs on hold position to help deny chargelots.

Control groups: Main army hotkey on 1. Ghosts, air units, your dropping medivacs, or tanks on 2. Try to not to F2 a-move as much when you are getting better at the game, you can watch how pro players choose to hotkey on streams or Youtube videos if they aren't hidden.

title: Battlefield 1: Great Visuals, Appropriate Themes, but Some Balance Issues
content:
My BF1 Profile

Battlefield 1 might be one of the best FPS games ever made, and even in the year 2025, there is still a moderate daily playerbase in the 1000s on Steamcharts. The cinematic videos are not too far off from actual gameplay, as in the visual details: shaders, textures, and terrain are all visually stunning. Effects aren't as realistic, but the explosions and footsteps help make up for average fire/explosion effects. Most buildings are fully destructible from direct tank shelling or bombers, and the collapse animation physics helps contribute to the immersive battlefield experience. The majority of the maps, for example Monte Grappa and Passchendaele, have a distinct immersive feel the first time you play on them. Fort De Vaux, Amiens, and Suez are also some visually appealing maps. Because BF1 is based on World War 1, the map design's account for historical accuracy is a step up from the more fictional battlegrounds in modern warfare games or futuristic titles. BF1 doesn't have the best maps, I have played some better lookings map on Enlisted, especially on the Normandy Campaign and the Battle for Berlin/Stalingrad maps. It's sad that Enlisted has some clunky sprinting movement, with the mechanics of Bf1 Enlisted's maps would definitely help make a combined title stand out. Even though Battlefield 5's maps, based on WW2 were technically designed to be more accurate, the gameplay felt boring since you had to trek across half of the map just to reach a middle point.

Mechanics: Battlefield 1 has had some complaints of being a run and gun type of game, especially on maps like Fort De Vaux or Prise de Tahure. The familiar three lane flanking routes and linear gameplay on those smaller maps are more like Call of Duty, but the starting areas look and feel realistic in a sense. From a spectator's viewpoint with the Heads Up Display disabled, the game looks great from a cinematic standpoint, for example on Argonne or Suez.

However, balance is the greatest downside of Bf1. Although from a designer's point of view the run and gun style of BF1 makes sense to compete with CoD Modern Warfare, the gameplay feels extremely off at times when you have to face an experienced veteran tank player or attack helicopter player with 150 service stars. For clarity, it takes 100 kills to gain 1 service star for any class of weapon/vehicle in the game. What ends up happening is that most of the game lobbies nowadays have multiple veteran players, who are playing for kills and end up being really disheartening for newer players looking for an immersive experience rather than just getting kills or winning the matches.

Autorepair: awful design for infantry, easy gameplay for vehicle players. Generally, vehicle players prefer choosing vehicles while fps gamers like to play the simple assuault class infantry. However, vehicles are awfully balanced in BF1 when in the hands of a veteran player. First of all, medium tanks take a minimum of 3 anti-tank grenades to destroy, which might make realistic sense, but even light tanks take atleast 2 anti-tank grenades to explode. Bullets do zero damage to tanks, with the slight exception of a tankgewehr special class or sniper k-bullets, which barely do any damage to even light tanks. It doesn't make sense how a single tank can plow through a field of infantry if they maintain their distance and fire from a range beforehand. Anti tank grenades don't throw further than 20 meters, so all it takes is a tank to camp a chokepoint from a 50 meter distance to be unkillable by infantry. For fighter airplanes, the stationary anti-air turrets have to directly hit 8 flak shells to even take down a single plane. An experienced fighter pilot can just strafe and sweep through once every 20-30 seconds, and they will be untouchable, with the exception of other enemy pilots. So if the enemy team has a good tank or pilot, and your team doesn't, the game is essentially lost on the maps with low cover and wide-open point spaces. Even worse, the auto-repair mechanic tanks/airplanes allows pilots to reapir damaged vehicles good as new with no limit. Tanks also require 3 direct tank shots to kill, so good luck trying to prevent tanks from auto-repairing everytime they get hit once.

Gunplay: Kind of Bad. Battlefield 1 guns have few if any recoil, especially on shotguns. This essentially means that two players fighting with automatic weapons at 10 meters is determined completely by luck or the random spread of the weapon. Moreover, automatic weapon headshot damage is heavily nerfed in BF1. An mp40 takes over 4 headshots after A 25m dropoff to even take down a player, which is incredibly frustrating to play with. Even revolver headshots don't immediately drop your opponent after a 10m dropoff, you have to carefully aim two times and hit two separate headshots to even claim a headshot kill. Snipers, however can mostly one shot headshot within the damage dropoff range of 70 meters. Certain semi-auto rifles in the Medic class can also two shot headshot <20m. However in real life not even a heavy ballistic helmet could survive a rifle caliber bullet.

Spotting flares: a gamebreaking mechanic. Snipers have the option to equip a spot flare gun, which shoots up to ~40m in one direction, but reveals a ~120m radius on the minimap that shows where moving players are for your entire team to see. The problem is that the spot flare is basically wallhacks, hiding in a building won't save a player unless they have the inconspicuous perk and do not move at all. As a result, flanking and playing strategically gets shut down completely by a single flare. This mechanic would not be an issue if the main player mode was hardcore with no heads up display minimap, but unfortunately 64 player conquest is the main played mode in multiplayer servers. In addition, pressing 'q' instantly spots a visible enemy player and marks them on the minimap for your entire team, so good luck running in the middle opening of a choke. I won't go into other annoyances like gas nades or support resupply grenade spam on Fort, you will quickly see what I am talking about when you experience it in-game.Passchendaele

In conclusion, BF1 could have been, or be, the greatest FPS game even today, if the developers tweaked vehicles to be more fragile, bullet damage ot be more realistic, and spotting to be less invasive.

title: Steroid Users on Social Media and Body Dysmorphia
content:
Fake Natty

Do you go to the gym? Do you recognize several guys at the gym that seem to be there every day of the week? At seemingly random times of the day? Chances are atleast one of those people are on steroids, or performance enhancing drugs, SARMS, anabolics, testosterone, HGH. Particularly those who have proportionally large upper delts, traps, and shoulders. If not, then theres a 99% chance you have seen atleast one 'fitness influencer' on Instagram that looks big but is on anabolic steroids. These Instagram portfolios are based on how the user looks, and promote their own account through gym supplement sponsorships and merchandise. For the younger generation, having these profiles show up on their social media feeds is problematic, as some insecure individuals might feel what is called body dysmorphia, or having compelling OCD-like thoughts that lowers one's self esteem and compels one to eat less or go to the gym frequently, with unrealistic or natural standards. Having larger muscles might look better, but it makes the heart work harder. The dark side of anabolic abuse is decreased lifespan and early heart failure in bodybuilders. However, TRT, or testosterone replacement therapy, might be a more safer option for male individuals over the age of 50 when testosterone levels start to decline or have noticeably declined already.

If you're still unsure if someone is on steroids, identify if someone has low body fat, capped shoulders, and large upper deltoid muscles. From the reference picture it's clear that this individual has all three in addition to defined vascularity in the arms, which is a common indicator of low body fat and subsequent steroid use. This person's upper arms look almost bigger than his upper pecs or chest muscles.

title: How to Identify AI-Generated Content
content:
AI Generated Trump

Identifying AI-generated content online is necessary knowledge akin to recognizing online scams or identifying fraud. Since artificial intelligence software has the ability to generate text, images, and videos, it's important to understand how to identify content that is artificially edited. Although video editing is not necessarily used to mislead users, the quality of eye-catching thumbnails and flashy details is usually artificially boosted in a way that can be disingenuous.

First of all, movie studios have used CGI and computer-generated SFX effects for movies and videos for a a while now. It's entirely fair for movies to employ semi-realistic looking effects/sounds for entertainment purposes. However, compared to movie studios, NASA also uses computer image generation to develop conglomerated sattelite image data of the Earth. For scientific purposes, it would be disingenuous and misleading to employ fake microscope footage of bacteria, as an example.

There is a current problem with Facebook posts such that many of the top liked public posts are completely falsified and generated with chatGPT or artificial intelligence. You might have noticed a post or two along the lines of: 'My Great Grandmother/Grandfather in the 1900s' and a non-color image of some person that looked like it was from the past. The distinction is quite simple if you compare one of the fake old/historical images with ones from the past; the fake old/historical images are always high definition, with little image pixelation or blurry facial features. Truly old historical photos, due to their age, are usually found or uploaded online as low-definition pictures, with a dull look and slightly grainy texture. Facial features might be darker, the background may have multiple dark spots with no distinct shadows, and you would never consider the photo to be photoshopped, even if it were professionally restored and/or archived in a musuem. If you are still unsure if a Facebook image is fake, usually someone in the comments section bright enough will point out that it is. Another way to describe AI-generated posts is having a cartoonish kind of lighting/shadows akin to a watercolor painting whilst trying to appear natural even though the image is too high enough definition to be possibly real. You could try to think of it as the difference between a fast food commercial and the burgers you get in real life. A video editor or photoshop user would be able to zoom in on individual pixel clusters to see how smooth the colors are; AI-generated color images seem to like using layers of deep tone colors similar to how someone would use foundation on their face to appear more tan.

Articles and post content on the internet generated through chatGPT are also easily distinguishable if you can identify several defining characteristics. For storied content, AI will often employ em dashes or long hyphens '—' to show suspense in a story. Furthermore, these em dashes will appear as a slight pause in the middle of a sentence, similar to a TED Talk or someone giving a lecture/presentation. Normally, people don't pause when they are talking in the middle of a sentence unless they are trying to remember something or are looking for a response. Another characteristic of AI-generated story posts on Reddit is general formatting. Usually in a Reddit post, the author of the post will write in a conversational/casual tone that is easy to read and relate to. For example, TLDR stands for 'Too Long, Didn't Read', implying that posts that are too long and confounded are not important enough to read entirely. A normal Reddit or online forum post will sound like someone's genuine experience, interest, or question in a certain topic. Real posts are usually short and simple, unless someone is frustrated or extremely upset as something, of course it would make sense to exxagerate to show more emotion. However, life isn't a drama tv show series, so you can't really cry and whine online as you would not on the internet.

If you think of a video documentary or technology news article on Medium or Wired Magazine, this is another way to distinguish fake posts. Each starting line paragraph of the documentary or article will introduce or bring up a different topic that logically relates to the previous text. For example, 'Why did the duck cross the road?' would be followed by, ->

'To reach the river where it can go for a swim'.

'The duck had not been in the water for a while now. It's feathers began to feel dry, exacerbated by the glowing sunlight that had been being absorbed by the pavement for hours on end.
